Issued at 125 AM CST Fri Nov 13 2026

A single, dominant lake effect band stretches nearly down the
entire fetch of Lake Michigan early this morning with upstream 
radars largely overshooting the shallow convective cloud depths 
across the northern reaches of the lake. A quick-moving 
shortwave continues to drop southward out of Wisconsin, and is 
delivering a surge of colder mid/upper-level temperatures (500 
mb temps analyzed near -30 C across southern Wisconsin). This in
turn is resulting in increasing lake-induced thermodynamics 
with equilibrium heights progged nearing 12-14 kft which 
generally matches radar returns showing cloud tops nearing 
similar heights over the mid lake. The lake thermodynamics will 
peak from late tonight through early this afternoon before 
gradually diminishing through Friday night and Saturday morning.


Near surface convergence is quite intense at this time, with
slow veering noted in observation trends across western lower 
Michigan and persistent gusty northwesterly winds on the western
side of the lake. While earlier guidance was having some 
difficulty handling the location of the primary convergence 
axis, latest high-res guidance is generally doing a better job 
with near-term trends. With the passage of the aforementioned 
shortwave aloft veered low-level flow across the southern end of
the lake, expecting the lake band to make a gradual westward 
push towards the Illinois shore through late tonight and into 
the early morning hours. 

Have recently noted a few mPing reports of a rain/snow mix 
developing across interior portions of Lake County, Indiana
where surface wetbulb temperatures have started to cool towards
36 degrees, although will note the transition has been slower
than earlier guidance would have suggested. Expectation is for 
the rain/snow mix area to gradually expand over the next few 
hours (away from the immediate lake front) and eventually 
transition to all snow, particularly on the western portions of 
the band where surface temperatures are coldest. 

It's always difficult pinpointing exactly where these lake
effect bands will move, particularly with the potential for 
embedded meso-lows. However, the latest high-res guidance suite
remains steadfast in suggesting the longest duration of 
precipitation setting up in the vicinity of the IL/IN state line
around the eastern Will, western Lake (IN), and far SE Cook 
county border regions or thereabouts. Marginal surface 
temperature profiles (wetbulb temperatures generally in the mid 
30s) and a warm antecedent ground will tend to limit snow 
accumulations in an otherwise highly favorable environment for 
intense snowfall rates through this morning. Indeed, it will 
take the presence of intense snowfall rates to result in 
any meaningful accumulations as snow will slowly melt when/as 
rates ease. As such, long-duration snow accumulation output is 
likely not a representative solution for most of the area, as 
additional melting will take place this afternoon as 
temperatures warm into the upper 30s. 

In the heart of the heaviest part of the lake effect snow band,
the potential exists for a hyper-localized corridor of 
potentially more significant accumulations north of 5 inches, 
but this if only IF high snowfall rates remain persistent for 
more than a few hours this morning. At this time, the areal 
extent of this higher snowfall threat looks to be much too small
to meaningfully capture in the gridded forecast, and it's still
not totally clear this will materialize given the already- 
mentioned marginal thermal profiles. Latest forecast remains 
largely similar to the late-evening update, with a general 2-4 
inch swath across SE Cook, eastern Will, and western Lake 
Counties, and even so, most accumulations may end up relegated 
to elevated or grassy surfaces. Did also gently expand some 
light accumulations farther south into eastern Kankakee County 
and also farther inland towards Kendall/Grundy/eastern 
Livingston counties as there will be a potential for more inland
movement of the band this morning as low-level lapse rates 
steepen. 

While lake effect precip will continue this afternoon, any 
additional accumulations look to be minor and relegated to
grassy surfaces. This will result in a transition back to a 
rain/snow mix or all rain in most locations. Lake thermodynamics
will still support periods of heavier precipitation into this 
evening and early overnight, but the potential for persistent 
heavy snowfall rates will diminish. As such, while additional 
slushy accumulations are possible this evening, potential for 
hazardous travel conditions appears too low to justify extending
the Winter Weather Advisory through the night, particularly 
given the potential for melting this afternoon. 

Surface flow will veer and the low-levels will dry out through 
Saturday morning, with lingering lake effect ending through
Saturday afternoon across Porter County. Thereafter, conditions
